caption_hook: Rhode Island is tiny, but it holds ice-age leftovers, an old coal basin and a drifted-in continent.

layers.name: BLOCK ISLAND MORAINE
layers.what: The ice sheet stopped at the coast and dumped its load of clay, sand and boulders. Waves have since trimmed that pile into the steep cliffs of Block Island.
layers.bonus: Mohegan Bluffs rise about 150 feet above the beach and keep eroding.

layers.name: WESTERLY GRANITE
layers.what: Magma cooled slowly underground into a fine, evenly grained granite. Quarried near Westerly since the 1800s, it was carved into countless monuments and gravestones across the country.
layers.bonus: Its steady grain makes it a standard rock for lab experiments on how rocks break.

layers.name: RHODE ISLAND FORMATION
layers.hook: A swampy basin full of plants
layers.what: Rivers and swamps filled a sinking basin around today's Narragansett Bay with sand, mud and rotting plants. Crushed and cooked later, those plants became coal and left fossil ferns in the rock.
layers.bonus: Its coal got so squeezed and heated that it partly turned to graphite, so it was hard to burn.

layers.name: PURGATORY CONGLOMERATE
layers.what: Fast, flooding rivers dumped coarse pebbles and cobbles that hardened into conglomerate. At Purgatory Chasm in Middletown, waves and frost have split the rock into a narrow gorge by the sea.
layers.bonus: The pebbles come in many rock types, a record of how wild those old floods were.

layers.name: THE BASEMENT
layers.what: Much of the state sits on a strip of crust called Avalonia, which began near Africa and later fused onto North America. Its ancient granite and gneiss lie beneath the younger layers.
layers.bonus: The same drifted-in crust shows up in coastal Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Maine.
